items.prompt: Which two things should most error messages tell the reader?
choices: What happened and what to do next
The error code and the server name
Who is at fault and when it will be fixed
items.explanation: Readers need the fact and a way forward. Codes and blame help neither.

items.prompt: A shop door says only "Closed." What is missing?
choices: A bigger font and a bolder border
A friendly emoji
A reason and a next step
items.explanation: Without a reason or a return time, the reader cannot decide what to do.

items.prompt: A message that states a failure but gives no next step is best called:
choices: Too long to read
A dead end
Too warm in tone
items.explanation: The reader learns something went wrong and is left to guess the rest.

items.prompt: When is it worth including the cause of a failure?
choices: When knowing it changes what the reader does
Always, in full technical detail
Never, since it only confuses readers
items.explanation: A cause earns its words when it changes the reader's next move.

items.prompt: Who usually writes a weak error string like "Transaction failed"?
choices: A UX writer after a long design review
The reader's own browser
A developer filling in a placeholder
items.explanation: Often no one wrote it on purpose: a placeholder in an error branch shipped.

items.prompt: Which of these is microcopy?
choices: A five-page user manual
The text on a button or in a field hint
A quarterly marketing email
items.explanation: Microcopy is the small functional text inside the interface.

items.prompt: What is the main flaw of "Error 402: Transaction failed."?
choices: No usable cause and no next step
It states something untrue about the card
It is far too polite
items.explanation: It is accurate, but gives the reader nothing to act on.

items.prompt: What does UX writing add to a placeholder string?
choices: A longer message with more technical detail
A way to hide the failure from users
Text written on purpose for the reader
items.explanation: The practice is writing the words deliberately instead of by accident.

items.prompt: A file upload fails because the file is over a 10 MB limit. Which message follows the what-happened-plus-next-step pattern?
choices: This file is over the 10 MB limit. Choose a smaller file.
Upload failed due to an error. Please contact support for help.
Something went wrong with your upload. Please try once more.
Upload failed (code U-17). The system could not complete it.
items.explanation: Only the first names the cause and offers a next step the reader can take right now. The others are vague, push the work to support, or repeat the failure.
items.reference:
Anatomy of a useful error
📌 What happened, as a plain fact
➡️ What the reader can do next
🔎 Why, only if it changes that next move
🚪 "Closed." vs "Closed for lunch. Back at 2:00."
Why: a message earns its words by changing what the reader does next; a bare announcement of failure is a dead end.
items.learnMore:
Facts alone do not help

Two messages can both be true. The helpful one gives the reader something to do with the truth: a cause they recognise and a step they can take.

Common mistake

Treating a technically accurate message as finished. Accuracy is the minimum, not the goal.
items.reflection: Think of a sign or notification that left you stuck. What single added phrase would have told you what to do next?

items.prompt: A message says exactly which bank rule rejected a payment but offers no action. Which edit adds the most value?
choices: Add a firm apology at the start of the message, before the cause.
Add a friendly emoji to soften the cold tone.
Add the internal rule identifier at the end.
Add a sentence telling the reader what to try next.
items.explanation: The cause is already there; the missing piece is the way forward. An apology, an identifier, or an emoji leaves the reader just as stuck.

items.prompt: A login fails. Which cause statement is worth its words because it changes what the reader does?
choices: The authentication service returned a rejection code.
Your credentials could not be verified at this time.
The password is wrong. Check caps lock or reset it.
An error occurred while processing your sign-in.
items.explanation: Naming the likely cause (the password) points to two concrete moves. The others describe the failure without changing what the reader would do.

items.prompt: Which wording names the reader as the culprit?
choices: "Dates need the form 31/12/2026."
"You entered an invalid date."
"That date format is not recognised."
items.explanation: Starting with "You entered" assigns fault. The others describe the rule or the format.

items.prompt: Neutral wording keeps the subject on:
choices: The rule or the system
The reader's mistake
The developer who wrote it
items.explanation: Neutral messages talk about what went wrong, not who did it.

items.prompt: Which is the less blaming rewrite of "Your upload was too large"?
choices: "You must pick a smaller file."
"Your file is wrong."
"Files can be up to 10 MB."
items.explanation: Stating the limit is neutral and also tells the reader what to fix.

items.prompt: Why does blame hurt a message?
choices: It makes the message too short
The reader defends themselves instead of fixing it
It breaks the layout of the page
items.explanation: Defensiveness uses the energy the reader needed to solve the problem.

items.prompt: Neutral wording that states the rule also gives:
choices: A built-in next step
A longer loading time
A guarantee the error is fixed
items.explanation: If the rule is visible, the fix is nearly obvious.

items.prompt: "That format isn't quite right" compared with "Invalid value" is:
choices: Colder and more technical in tone
Longer but less clear
Gentler and about the format
items.explanation: It points at the format rather than labelling the input as bad.

items.prompt: Which words most often signal blame?
choices: "The format", "the limit", "this field"
"You entered", "you failed to"
"Try", "check"
items.explanation: Second-person past tense statements about a mistake point a finger.

items.prompt: A message can be neutral and still:
choices: Be fully accurate
Hide the real cause
Avoid giving an action
items.explanation: Neutral describes tone, so it can be completely truthful.

items.prompt: Which rewrite of "You entered an invalid phone number" removes blame and adds the rule?
choices: Phone numbers can contain digits only, with no spaces.
The phone number you typed in was not valid for this form.
Please correct the invalid phone number and resubmit.
You must enter a phone number in the proper form.
items.explanation: The first states the rule and has no accusing subject. The others keep "you" or "invalid" and leave the actual rule unstated.
items.reference:
Blame versus cause
👉 Blame: "You entered an invalid date."
📏 Neutral: "Dates need the form 31/12/2026."
🧩 The neutral version names the rule, so it carries its own fix
🛡️ Less defensiveness, more fixing
Why: neutral wording keeps attention on the problem, so the reader spends effort fixing it instead of defending themselves.
items.learnMore:
Subject of the sentence

Whoever or whatever is the grammatical subject gets the attention. Putting the rule or the system in that spot keeps the message about the problem.

Common mistake

Softening the adjective ('slightly invalid') while leaving the reader as the subject.
items.reflection: Recall feedback you received that made you defensive. How would it have read if the subject had been the work instead of you?

items.prompt: A form rejects a name longer than 40 characters. Which message is both neutral and actionable?
choices: You wrote a name that is much too long.
Your name is invalid because of its length, so shorten it.
Names are limited to 40 characters. Please shorten it.
An invalid name was entered in the first field.
items.explanation: It states the limit as a fact about the form and implies the fix. The others assign fault or only announce invalidity.

items.prompt: Which change turns "Your password is too weak" into a neutral message with a next step?
choices: Write "Your password is really far too weak" instead.
Write "The password you chose was not strong."
Write "Weak passwords are not accepted here."
Write "Use 12 or more characters and one number."
items.explanation: Giving the rule makes the fix visible and drops the verdict on the reader. Tweaking the adjective keeps the judgement.

items.prompt: Which three questions can an error message answer?
choices: Who, what, when, and where
Cause, impact, action
Title, body, footer
items.explanation: The triad is what happened, what it means for me, what to do.

items.prompt: Which of the three is never worth skipping?
choices: The action
The internal error code
The apology
items.explanation: Without an action the message is a dead end.

items.prompt: "Invalid input" next to a field already outlined in red mostly:
choices: Explains the rule that was broken
Gives a next step
Repeats what the reader sees
items.explanation: The border already says the field is wrong; the text adds nothing.

items.prompt: "Try again." on its own answers which question?
choices: Cause only
Action only
Impact only
items.explanation: It says what to do but not why, so the reader may repeat the mistake.

items.prompt: When should a message state the impact?
choices: When the consequence is non-obvious or costly
Every time, in a separate sentence
Never, readers can infer it
items.explanation: Say it when data loss or a charge might surprise the reader.

items.prompt: Impact can be skipped when:
choices: The message is already quite long
The cause is unknown
The consequence is obvious
items.explanation: Saying 'nothing was saved' next to an empty field adds nothing.

items.prompt: A cause specific enough to imply the action means:
choices: The message must be longer
No separate action sentence is needed
The tone can be playful
items.explanation: "Passwords need 8+ characters" already says what to fix.

items.prompt: Cause with no action is:
choices: Informative but a dead end
The strongest possible message
The same as 'Try again'
items.explanation: The reader learns what happened and still has to guess the fix.

items.prompt: A save fails because the reader's disk quota is full. Which message uses cause, impact and action together?
choices: Save failed. Please try saving your document again in a moment or two.
An error occurred while writing data. Contact support.
Your storage is full, so these edits were not saved. Free up space.
Storage quota exceeded. The save operation was cancelled.
items.explanation: It names the cause, states the costly impact (edits not saved), and gives a fix. Retrying would hit the same full disk.
items.reference:
The triad
🔍 Cause: what happened (nearly always, briefly)
💥 Impact: what it means (when non-obvious or costly)
👉 Action: what to do (always)
🎯 A specific cause can imply the action
Why: each question has a rule for when it earns words, and a message with no action leaves the reader stuck.
items.learnMore:
Spend words where they change behaviour

A twelve-word message cannot answer everything. The triad is a budget: cause almost always, impact when the stakes are not obvious, action every time.

Common mistake

Adding an apology or reassurance in place of the missing cause or action.
items.reflection: Pick an error you hit this week. Which of the three questions did it leave unanswered, and what did that cost you?

items.prompt: A field error says "Try again." for a username already taken. What is the strongest repair?
choices: Add the word please before the instruction to try again.
Add the system's reason code after the instruction.
Say the username is taken and ask for a different one.
Replace the text with the single word invalid.
items.explanation: Naming the cause makes the action meaningful. Retrying the same name fails again, whatever the politeness or code.

items.prompt: For which failure is a retry-only message most defensible?
choices: A brief network drop that usually clears on its own
A file that exceeds the maximum allowed size
A password that fails the minimum length rule
A user lacking permission to open the page
items.explanation: A retry works when the cause is temporary. The other three fail identically every time until the reader changes something.

items.prompt: As stakes for the reader rise, fitting tone gets:
choices: Cuter and more playful
Plainer and more precise
Shorter and more cryptic
items.explanation: High-stakes moments need calm, exact language.

items.prompt: Where is a light, warm tone most fitting?
choices: A mistyped search
A deleted account
A declined payment
items.explanation: Small, frequent, low-cost failures are where warmth fits.

items.prompt: Why does a cheerful emoji on a deletion warning backfire?
choices: It forces the whole page to reload again after each click on it
It hides the button label
It signals the product is relaxed about something serious
items.explanation: Tone should match what the reader stands to lose.

items.prompt: System voice describes what:
choices: The reader needs to know
The server experienced
The designer intended
items.explanation: A log line is written for an engineer, not the reader.

items.prompt: Which is the human-voice version of "Request failed with status 402"?
choices: "Your card was declined by your bank."
"Status 402 returned."
"The payment module raised an exception."
items.explanation: Human voice says what it means for the reader.

items.prompt: Warmth is best described as:
choices: A feature to maximise in every message everywhere
Something to avoid in all errors
A resource to spend on small failures
items.explanation: Spend it where cost is low and frequency is high.

items.prompt: An irreversible action calls for:
choices: A playful joke to ease the tension
Precise, serious wording
A very short message
items.explanation: The clearer the consequence, the fewer chances for an accident.

items.prompt: Tone and the triad are:
choices: Two separate axes
The same thing
Only relevant to long messages
items.explanation: The triad decides what is said; tone decides how.

items.prompt: Which confirmation text best fits permanently deleting a shared folder?
choices: Oops! Say goodbye to this folder! Ready to go?
Delete "Team Photos" for everyone? This cannot be undone.
Are you sure? You can always come back to this later.
Heads up: this will remove the folder, hope that's okay with you all!
items.explanation: It names the target and states irreversibility in a calm register. The others joke, reassure falsely, or stay vague about the stakes.
items.reference:
Stakes against warmth
🔎 Typo in a search: light, even warm
📝 Empty required field: plain and brief
💳 Payment declined: plain, calm
🗑️ Account deleted: precise, serious
Why: warmth is a resource spent where failures are small and frequent; as consequences grow, the writing gets plainer.
items.learnMore:
Voice and tone

Voice is who the message sounds like (a person, not a log). Tone is how serious it sounds. Both should be chosen against what the reader stands to lose.

Common mistake

Giving every error the same friendly register because it suits the brand.
items.reflection: Think of a time a brand's jokey tone annoyed you. What was at stake for you at that moment?

items.prompt: A product uses the same bouncy "Whoops!" opener on every error. What is the main design problem?
choices: Opener text makes every message too long for the reader to scan.
Readers cannot tell which messages are errors.
Bouncy tone cannot be translated well into most other languages.
Warmth fits small failures but sounds careless on costly ones.
items.explanation: Tone must track stakes. A uniform cheerful register is fine for a typo and tone-deaf for a failed payment or lost data.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly orders the fitting tone for "search typo" and "account deleted"?
choices: Both should use the same neutral tone throughout.
Search typo calmer, account deleted warmer.
Search typo lighter, account deleted plainer.
Both should be as playful as the brand allows.
items.explanation: Fitting warmth falls as consequence rises. The low-stakes moment can be light; the irreversible one should be plain and exact.

items.prompt: The first step in rewriting a raw error is to:
choices: Name the cause category that changes the reader's move
Add a lengthy apology and a mention of the technical stack
Shorten the message to one word
items.explanation: The cause category decides what the reader will do next.

items.prompt: For "Error: Request failed.", a good cause is:
choices: "A timeout in the HTTP layer."
"You appear to be offline right now."
"We couldn't reach the server."
items.explanation: It is true across several failures and blames neither side.

items.prompt: Why not tell the reader if it was a timeout or a DNS failure?
choices: It would take too many words to explain properly
They would act the same way on both
It is illegal in many places
items.explanation: If the reader's response is identical, the distinction is noise.

items.prompt: In the four steps, step 2 asks:
choices: Is the impact non-obvious?
Is the logo visible?
Is the message translated?
items.explanation: Impact is only stated when the consequence is not already clear.

items.prompt: A failed page load is usually:
choices: Catastrophic and irreversible
Impossible to recover from
Annoying but low stakes
items.explanation: Plain, calm wording suits annoying-but-minor failures.

items.prompt: "Check your connection and try again" suits a network failure because:
choices: A retry never works for this failure
A retry is reasonable for it
It blames the reader
items.explanation: The cause is often temporary, so trying again is a sensible move.

items.prompt: Which wording blames neither side?
choices: "We couldn't reach the server."
"You seem to be offline right now."
"Our server is down."
items.explanation: The reader may be fine and the server may be fine; the message claims only what it knows.

items.prompt: The last of the four steps checks:
choices: The page title and its length
The font weight
Tone against stakes
items.explanation: Tone is judged against what the reader stands to lose.

items.prompt: A session expires while the reader fills in a long form. Which message applies all four steps correctly?
choices: You were signed out after inactivity. Sign in to continue; your answers were saved.
Error: Request failed. Please reload the page and then try entering your answers again.
Oops! Your session ran away from us. Click here to sign in again, friend!
Authentication token invalid. The request could not be completed at this time.
items.explanation: It names the real cause, states the costly impact, and gives the action, in a calm tone. (It is only correct if the answers really were saved.)
items.reference:
Four-step rewrite
1️⃣ Cause: the category that changes the reader's move
2️⃣ Impact: only if non-obvious or costly
3️⃣ Action: a concrete next step
4️⃣ Tone: checked against the stakes
Why: the steps force each sentence to earn its place by changing what the reader knows or does.
items.learnMore:
A procedure, not a mood

Rewriting works as four checks. Each checks one thing: cause category, impact, action, tone. Skipping a step usually shows up as one of the single-question failures from L2.

Common mistake

Naming the exact technical failure when the reader's response is the same for all of them.
items.reflection: Take a raw message you have seen in an app. Run the four steps on it and note which step changed it the most.

items.prompt: Why does the network-error rewrite skip an impact sentence, while the session-expiry rewrite should not?
choices: Network errors are always more serious than expiry.
Impact sentences are banned for any technical errors.
Impact is only stated when the consequence is non-obvious.
Session messages need to be longer than other messages by convention.
items.explanation: A page that visibly did not load needs no explanation. Possible loss of typed work is non-obvious, so it must be stated.

choices: Replace it with a one-word message, such as Failed, and stop there.
Identify the category that changes the reader's response.
Add an apology and keep the HTTP code in the text.
Explain how a server error gets produced internally.
items.explanation: The reader cannot act on "500". The useful category is whether the reader or the service is at fault, and what they can try.

items.prompt: A good destructive confirmation says what is destroyed and:
choices: Whether it can be undone
How fast the server will respond
Who clicked last
items.explanation: Reversibility is the second thing the reader needs to decide.

items.prompt: "Are you sure?" fails mainly because it:
choices: Is too long
Is too specific
Names nothing
items.explanation: The reader confirms blind.

items.prompt: Which version names the target?
choices: "Delete this item and all of its related content?"
"Delete 'Q3 Planning'? This can't be undone."
"Proceed?"
items.explanation: Only the first says what will be removed.

items.prompt: Is "Only project admins can delete this board." a cause?
choices: Yes, it is the rule that blocked the reader
No, it is only an action the reader can take now
No, it is only a tone choice
items.explanation: It states why the delete was refused.

items.prompt: When the reader cannot fix a permission error alone, the action becomes:
choices: Retry immediately
Nothing at all
Who to talk to
items.explanation: Asking an admin is still an action, just a human one.

items.prompt: A rate-limit message is clearer when it gives:
choices: Only the single word 'denied' alone
The limit and when it resets
The server's name
items.explanation: A fact and a time replace the worry of being banned.

items.prompt: "Too many requests." sounds like:
choices: The reader did something wrong
A friendly tip about slowing down
A confirmation
items.explanation: It states a problem without the rule.

items.prompt: A casual 'Cool with that? 😅' on an irreversible delete:
choices: Improves clarity for the reader
Adds reversibility
Undersells the stakes
items.explanation: Cute tone suggests the action is minor.

items.prompt: Which confirmation for removing a customer list is best?
choices: Remove "Spring Customers" and its 230 contacts? This cannot be undone.
Whoops, this will wipe the list! Cool with that? Press yes to nuke it.
Are you sure you want to continue with the removal of this list?
This action is permanent and may affect various contacts in the list.
items.explanation: It names the target and size, and states irreversibility plainly. (The list name and count are example copy.) The others are vague, casual, or leave out the target.
items.reference:
Destructive actions
🎯 Name exactly what will be destroyed
↩️ State plainly whether it can be undone
🙅 No blame, no false cheer
🔑 For permissions: name the rule and who can help
Why: a confirmation is a decision; it must carry the two facts the reader needs to make that decision.
items.learnMore:
Confirming blind

A generic confirmation technically asks for a decision but gives nothing to reason with. The good version is longer only because it answers the two questions that matter: what, and can I get it back.

Common mistake

items.prompt: A rate limit hits a reader. Which message best replaces the anxiety of "Too many requests"?
choices: You are sending too many requests; please slow down your use.
Request denied: limit exceeded for this account on its current plan tier.
Hold on a moment! You seem very busy, so take a short break.
You have reached 100 searches this hour. It resets in 12 minutes.
items.explanation: A concrete limit and reset time turn a vague accusation into a plain fact. (The numbers are example copy.)

items.prompt: A reader without rights tries to delete a board. What should the message do?

Apologise warmly and tell them to try again later.
Hide the delete button and show nothing at all.

items.explanation: The reader cannot fix this alone, so the action is a person to contact. Retrying will fail the same way every time.

items.prompt: Which cause should a message state?
choices: The most technically complete cause that the logs contain
The one that is shortest

items.explanation: The test is use to the reader, not completeness.

items.prompt: A reader cannot clear a fraud flag from a checkout page, so a message should:
choices: Describe the flag in detail
Focus on what they can do
Say nothing at all
items.explanation: Lead with actionable wording.

items.prompt: Naming 'suspected fraud' to a legitimate customer can read as:
choices: An accusation
A routine reminder
A discount
items.explanation: It sounds like the reader is under suspicion.

items.prompt: A softer wording of a cause must still be:
choices: Funny
Very long
True
items.explanation: Replacing a cause with an invented one is dishonest.

items.prompt: Where can the exact error code live?
choices: Nowhere, since it should be deleted
Somewhere available to support
At the top as a headline
items.explanation: Keep it accessible but do not lead with it.

items.prompt: "Your bank declined this card." is:
choices: True and actionable
False and reassuring
True but useless
items.explanation: It names a cause the reader can respond to.

items.prompt: The message on screen is for:
choices: The logs first
The auditors first
The reader first
items.explanation: Support can use the code; the screen is for the person.

items.prompt: A cause that alarms and cannot be acted on should be replaced by:
choices: A made-up reassurance that sounds kind
The nearest actionable true cause
An empty message
items.explanation: Stay true, and stay useful.

items.prompt: The processor logs "issuer flagged transaction as suspected fraud". Which message to a customer is best?
choices: Your bank flagged this purchase as a case of suspected card fraud.
Your payment looks suspicious, so it was automatically stopped.
Your bank declined this card. Contact them, or try another card.
The payment failed. A security rule on your card applied.
items.explanation: It stays true, avoids implying suspicion, and keeps the action concrete. The others name or hint at the fraud flag.
items.reference:
Choosing the cause to show
🎯 Can the reader act on it? State it specifically
😟 Does it only alarm? Use the nearest actionable cause
✅ Whatever you say must be true
🧾 Keep the exact code available for support
Why: the right cause is the one the reader can act on or take comfort from, not the most technically complete one.
items.learnMore:
Specificity has a target

More detail is better only up to the point the reader can use it. Beyond that, it risks alarming them or burying the next step.

Common mistake

Treating the log's cause as the message's cause by default.
items.reflection: Think of a time you were given too much or too alarming detail. What would have been the most useful true thing to hear?

items.prompt: A teammate says to always show the exact error code as the cause. What is the best reply?
choices: Agreed, because completeness is the main quality of a cause.
Agreed, but only when the code is short enough to fit.
Disagree: show it only for admins and hide it from everyone else.
Disagree: lead with a usable cause and keep the code for support.
items.explanation: Accuracy for an engineer and usefulness for the reader differ. Leading with the cause the reader can use serves them; the code stays available to support.

items.prompt: Which softened cause crosses the line from kind to dishonest?
choices: Saying the bank declined the card when it did
Saying "a temporary glitch" when the card was refused
Leaving out an internal reason code from the text
Saying to contact the bank for the specific reason
items.explanation: Calling a refusal a glitch invents a cause. Omitting detail the reader cannot use is fine; stating something false is not.
